::: {.at-a-glance}
- **Time:** about 40 minutes, at home; best after [C Bash 101](C-bash.qmd).
- **You need:** a terminal and Pixi ([lesson 00](00-setup.qmd)).
- **You will have:** nano, tmux and screen installed, Git set to use nano, and a command that kept running after the shell that started it was gone.
:::

## Overview

### Why this matters

Sooner or later you will work where there is no graphical editor and no
window you can keep open: on a cluster such as Karakoram, in a GitHub
Codespace, in WSL2, on any computer you reach with `ssh`. Two skills make
that comfortable. The first is editing a file in the terminal itself. Git
even opens an editor by itself when it needs a message from you, and if that
editor is vim and you have never used it, you are stuck. The second is
keeping a long command running. A full pipeline run, a container build or a
large download can take an hour, and a command started in a terminal stops
when the terminal closes, the laptop sleeps or the connection drops. A
*terminal multiplexer* (tmux or screen) runs the command in a session of its
own, which you can leave and come back to.

### What you do in this lesson

You install nano, tmux and screen with Pixi, edit a file with nano and make
it Git's editor, learn the handful of vim keys that get you out of trouble,
and run commands in tmux and screen sessions that outlive their terminal.

### Learning outcomes

After this page you can:

1. **Edit** and save a file in the terminal with nano, and **set** it as the editor Git uses.
2. **Get out of** vim, saving or discarding your changes, when a program opens it.
3. **Run** a long command in a tmux or screen session, **detach**, and **reattach** later to see how it went.

Checks: your answers to *Try it yourself*, and section 4: the job inside
tmux survives what stops the job outside it.

## 1. Get the tools

nano, tmux and screen are small programs, but not every computer has them,
or has the same version. On macOS, for example, the `nano` command is really
pico, an older editor with the same basic keys, and there is no tmux.
Install all three with Pixi. It needs no administrator rights, so this also
works on a cluster ([lesson 05](05-pixi.qmd#personal-tools-with-pixi-global)):

```{.bash .run}
pixi global install nano tmux screen
```

Open a new terminal, so that it finds the new commands, then check:

```{.bash .run}
nano --version | head -n 1
tmux -V
```

```text
 GNU nano, version 9.3
tmux 3.8
```

Your versions may be newer. vim is already installed on macOS, Linux and
WSL2.

Make a folder for this page and go there:

```{.bash .run}
mkdir -p ~/cbio7501/terminal-practice
cd ~/cbio7501/terminal-practice
```

## 2. nano: an editor that shows its keys

Open a file (nano creates it if it does not exist):

```{.bash .norun}
nano notes.md
```

nano fills the terminal. Type a few lines, for example a heading and today's
date. The two lines at the bottom list the commands: `^` means the Ctrl key
and `M-` the Alt key, so `^O` is Ctrl-O.

| Keys | What it does |
|------|--------------|
| `Ctrl-O`, then Enter | save (*write out*) under the name shown; change the name first to save a copy |
| `Ctrl-X` | exit; if there are unsaved changes, nano asks first (`Y` or `N`) |
| `Ctrl-W` (or `Ctrl-F` in nano 8 and later) | search; `Ctrl-W` and Enter again finds the next match |
| `Ctrl-K`, `Ctrl-U` | cut the current line, paste it |
| `Alt-U` | undo |
| `Ctrl-G` | help |

Save with `Ctrl-O` and Enter, leave with `Ctrl-X`, and look at the file from
the shell with `cat notes.md`.

On macOS, the Alt key only works in nano after one setting: in Terminal,
*Settings → Profiles → Keyboard → Use Option as Meta key*. Without it, press
Esc and then the letter.

### Make nano Git's editor

Git opens an editor when it needs text from you: a commit message if you run
`git commit` without `-m`, or a message for a merge after `git pull`. Unless
you choose one, that editor is often vim. Choose nano:

```{.bash .run-ci}
git config --global core.editor nano
git config --global core.editor
```

```text
nano
```

If you set up Git with [lesson 00](00-setup.qmd#tell-git-who-you-are)
recently, this is done already. Other programs use the editor named in the
`EDITOR` variable; to make nano their default too, add the line
`export EDITOR=nano` to `~/.zshrc` (macOS) or `~/.bashrc` (Linux, WSL2).

## 3. vim: the keys that get you out

vim is on almost every Unix computer, and many programs open it. It is
powerful, and confusing at first, because it has **modes**. In *normal* mode,
which is where vim starts, keys are commands: `x` deletes a character, `d`
starts a deletion. Only in *insert* mode do keys type text. That is why
typing into vim without knowing this seems to do strange things.

```{.bash .norun}
vim notes.md
```

| Keys | What it does |
|------|--------------|
| `i` | insert mode: now you can type |
| `Esc` | back to normal mode (press it whenever in doubt) |
| `:w`, then Enter | save |
| `:wq`, then Enter | save and quit |
| `:q!`, then Enter | quit **without** saving |
| `u` | undo (in normal mode) |
| `/word`, then Enter | search for *word*; `n` finds the next match |

::: {.callout-tip title="Stuck in vim?"}
Press `Esc`, type `:q!` and press Enter. You are out, and the file is
unchanged. If Git opened vim for a message you want to keep, type `:wq`
instead.
:::

vim comes with its own 30-minute tutorial, for when you want more than the
way out:

```{.bash .norun}
vimtutor
```

## 4. tmux: sessions that keep running

A command you start in a terminal belongs to that terminal. When the window
closes, or the `ssh` connection to a cluster drops, the terminal sends it a
*hang-up* signal and the command stops. tmux works differently: it runs a
small server in the background, your commands run in the server's
**sessions**, and your terminal only shows one of them. Close the terminal
and the session goes on; open a new terminal and **attach** to it again.

Start a session called `practice`:

```{.bash .norun}
tmux new -s practice
```

A green bar at the bottom shows that you are inside tmux. Run something slow,
a loop that counts for a minute:

```{.bash .norun}
for i in $(seq 1 60); do echo "step $i"; sleep 1; done
```

Now **detach**: press `Ctrl-b`, let go, then press `d`. You are back in your
normal terminal, and the loop is still counting inside the session. List the
sessions, and attach again to watch it finish:

```{.bash .norun}
tmux ls
tmux attach -t practice
```

Every tmux key starts with the *prefix* `Ctrl-b`:

| `Ctrl-b`, then | What it does |
|----------------|--------------|
| `d` | detach |
| `[` | scroll back: arrows or Page Up and Down; `q` leaves |
| `c`, `n`, `p` | new window, next window, previous window |
| `%`, `"` | split the window side by side, or top and bottom; `Ctrl-b` and an arrow moves between the parts |
| `?` | list all keys |

`exit` in the last window ends the session. To scroll with the mouse, put the
line `set -g mouse on` in a file called `~/.tmux.conf`.

### Without attaching

tmux can also start a session in the background and show you what is on its
screen, without taking over your terminal. This is handy in scripts, and it
is how the tests of this page check tmux:

```{.bash .run}
tmux new-session -d -s counting 'for i in $(seq 1 30); do echo "step $i"; sleep 1; done'
sleep 3
tmux ls
tmux capture-pane -p -t counting | grep step | tail -n 1
tmux kill-session -t counting
```

```text
counting: 1 windows (created Mon Oct 26 20:46:25 2026)
step 3
```

`-d` starts the session detached, `capture-pane -p` prints what the session
shows, and `kill-session` ends it.

### Why tmux: one job dies, one survives

See the hang-up signal (`HUP`) at work. Send it yourself, as a closing
terminal would, to a command running in the background (`&`) of this shell:

```{.bash .run}
sleep 300 &
job=$!
kill -HUP "$job"
sleep 1
```

`$!` is the process number of the last command started with `&`. Is the job
still running? `kill -0` asks, without doing anything to it:

```{.bash .expect-fail}
kill -0 "$job"
```

```text
bash: kill: (12345) - No such process
```

(zsh, the macOS shell, says `kill: kill 12345 failed: no such process`.) The
job is gone. That is what happens to a pipeline run when the laptop closes or
the connection drops.

Now start the same job in a tmux session, from a shell that ends right away,
as a closed terminal would:

```{.bash .run}
bash -c 'tmux new-session -d -s survivor "sleep 300"'
tmux ls
```

```text
survivor: 1 windows (created Mon Oct 26 20:46:29 2026)
```

The shell that started it is gone; the job is not, because it belongs to the
tmux server. Clean up:

```{.bash .run}
tmux kill-session -t survivor
```

### In practice

With the LTEE project, a long run looks like this. On a cluster, log in with
`ssh` first.

```{.bash .norun}
tmux new -s pipeline
cd ~/cbio7501/ltee-project
pixi run reproduce
# Ctrl-b d, close the laptop, go home; later, in a new terminal:
tmux attach -t pipeline
```

A tmux session lives on the computer where you started it. On a cluster
with several login nodes, note which one with `hostname`, and log in to the
same node to attach. Heavy computations belong in jobs on the cluster's
compute nodes, not on the login node: tmux keeps the command that *submits*
the jobs alive, such as Snakemake with a cluster profile
([lesson 09](09-snakemake.qmd)).

## 5. screen: the older alternative

Some computers have screen but not tmux. It works the same way, with
`Ctrl-a` as the prefix:

| What you want | tmux | screen |
|---------------|------|--------|
| start a named session | `tmux new -s NAME` | `screen -S NAME` |
| detach | `Ctrl-b d` | `Ctrl-a d` |
| list sessions | `tmux ls` | `screen -ls` |
| attach again | `tmux attach -t NAME` | `screen -r NAME` |
| scroll back | `Ctrl-b [` (`q` leaves) | `Ctrl-a [` (`Esc` leaves) |
| end a session from outside | `tmux kill-session -t NAME` | `screen -S NAME -X quit` |

Try it in the background, as with tmux:

```{.bash .run}
screen -dmS counting sleep 30
screen -ls | grep counting
screen -S counting -X quit
```

```text
	12345.counting	(Detached)
```

`-dm` starts the session detached, `-S` names it, and `-X quit` sends it the
command to end.

## Try it yourself

1. You opened a file in vim, typed, and now the text is full of strange
   changes. How do you leave without saving any of them?

   ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
   `Esc`, then `:q!` and Enter.
   :::

2. In nano, how do you find the word `depth` in a long file, and how do you
   save the file under a new name?

   ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
   `Ctrl-W`, type `depth`, Enter (`Ctrl-W` and Enter again for the next
   match). To save under a new name: `Ctrl-O`, change the name shown, Enter.
   :::

3. You started a long run in tmux on a cluster, then your connection
   dropped. What do you type after you log in again?

   ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
   `tmux ls` to see the session's name, then `tmux attach -t NAME`. If
   `tmux ls` finds nothing, check with `hostname` that you are on the same
   login node as before.
   :::

4. Start a tmux session with two parts side by side: `top` in one, a shell
   in the other. Which keys do you need?

   ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
   `tmux new -s watch`, then `Ctrl-b %` to split, `top` in one part, and
   `Ctrl-b` with an arrow key to move to the other. `q` leaves `top`.
   :::

## Troubleshooting

| Problem | What to do |
|---------|------------|
| `command not found` for nano, tmux or screen after `pixi global install` | Open a new terminal. If it still fails, check that `~/.pixi/bin` is in your `PATH` (`echo $PATH`); the Pixi installer adds it ([lesson 00](00-setup.qmd)). |
| Typing in vim does strange things | You are in normal mode. Press `Esc`, then `:q!` and Enter to leave without saving. |
| nano's `M-` (Alt) keys do nothing on macOS | Turn on *Use Option as Meta key* (section 2), or press Esc and then the letter. |
| `sessions should be nested with care` | You are already inside tmux. Detach first (`Ctrl-b d`), or open another window with `Ctrl-b c`. |
| `no server running` or `no sessions` | No tmux session runs on this computer: it ended, the computer restarted, or you are on another login node of the cluster (`hostname`). |
| `can't find session` | Check the name with `tmux ls`. |
| `No Sockets found` from `screen -ls` | No screen session runs for you on this computer. |
| A session on the cluster disappears after some hours | Some clusters end long processes on login nodes. Run the heavy work as jobs, and ask the cluster's documentation whether tmux is allowed there. |

## Apply it to your own project

Two habits for your capstone. Commit once with `git commit` and no `-m`, so
nano opens: write a short summary line, an empty line, then why you made the
change. And run the longest step of your own analysis inside tmux, so a
closed laptop does not cost you the run.

## Key points

- nano shows its keys at the bottom: `Ctrl-O` saves, `Ctrl-X` exits. Make it Git's editor with `git config --global core.editor nano`.
- In vim, `Esc` then `:wq` saves and quits; `Esc` then `:q!` quits without saving.
- A command started in a terminal stops when the terminal closes or the connection drops; inside tmux or screen it keeps running.
- tmux: `tmux new -s NAME`, detach with `Ctrl-b d`, list with `tmux ls`, come back with `tmux attach -t NAME`. screen: `screen -S NAME`, `Ctrl-a d`, `screen -ls`, `screen -r NAME`.
